<reason>Both sides built coherent, well-supported cases and pressed each other hard, but A maintained a tighter throughline: the environment-versus-willpower/equity mechanism introduced in the opening was reused consistently through rebuttals and the closing "who never gets in the room" argument. When B's Pressure Question forced A to admit no jurisdiction has reduced obesity via environmental policy, A's parry ("name one for coaching either") was effective because B's own rebuttal never actually named a population-scale success either, only individual-trial data — leaving that exchange closer to a wash than B's closing implied. B's case was rich with concrete real-world examples (Mexico, Denmark, Britain, Chile) and landed a sharp catch on A's inconsistent listing/disowning of calorie labeling, but B's own model wavered between "intensive coaching" and "universal schools," slightly undercutting its scalability argument, and B's speeches were clipped twice for exceeding word limits, costing content and execution credit. A's closing "in the people they reach" line was answered cleverly by B's "universal coverage of a null effect" retort, but that retort mainly rescued the schools example rather than the broader coaching claims A had been attacking throughout, so A's core equity/reach critique survives more intact than B's null-effect critique of environmental policy.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>The clash over B's Pressure Question ("name one jurisdiction where environmental policy reduced obesity" [B3.1]) and A's answer ("name one for population-scale coaching either" [A4.1]), later echoed in the closings' dueling use of the phrase "reach" [A5.1/B5.1], was the most decisive exchange — it exposed that neither side has a completed population-scale success story, and how each side spun that mutual gap determined the final framing of the debate.</best_rebuttal>
